---
title: "Lab 2 — One case, three outputs"
subtitle: "Day Two · 35 min"
---

Module 4 gave you a technique: write the facts down once, then draw every output from that one sheet. Module 5 gave you a habit: check the numbers against a source. This lab uses both, one step at a time. You make three outputs for three readers, and after each one you check the same three facts against the sheet. Never all three at once.

::: {.session-meta}
Time
:   35 minutes, three parts: one sheet, three outputs 20; same source, two tools 10; share-out 5

Slides
:   [Open the deck](../slides/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd): the same lab, one step to a slide, with the pictures.

Uses
:   [Case A](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-a) by default, any [case card](../reference/case-cards.qmd) allowed; the [practice source](../reference/practice-source.qmd) in part 2

You leave with
:   A source-of-truth sheet you checked yourself. A chart note, a patient handout, and a three-slide teaching version, with a nine-box table showing whether each kept the three facts. A second look at two ways of answering, on a Day Two task.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## On the call
You need three tabs: the call, the slides (your instructor pastes the link in the chat), and your general assistant, signed in. Copy each prompt from its slide with the Copy prompt button; your instructor pastes it in the chat too. Part 2 adds one more tab for your second option from Lab One ([Module 3](../day1/m3-choosing-tools.qmd#second-option)), for ten minutes. This page is the take-home version, and every prompt is also in the [prompt library](../reference/prompt-library.qmd). A tool misbehaving? See [troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The privacy line
No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop.
:::

Use a case card. If you bring a case of your own, apply the [privacy checklist](../reference/privacy-checklist.qmd) first, and if you are not certain it is safe, use a card.

## 1. One sheet, three outputs [20 min]{.time} {#part-1}

One event, three readers: the chart, the patient, and an audience of colleagues. The facts must not change as the words do. The way to keep them still is the sheet: build it once, check it once, and draw everything from it. Then make one output, check it, and only then make the next.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["Case card"] --> B["The sheet<br/>facts only, checked by you"]
    B --> C["Chart note<br/>for the record"]
    B --> D["Patient handout<br/>plain language"]
    B --> E["Three slides<br/>for colleagues"]
    classDef sheet fill:#EEF2FF,stroke:#4F46E5,stroke-width:3px,color:#0F172A
    classDef out fill:#CCFBF1,stroke:#14B8A6,color:#0F172A
    classDef src fill:#F1F5F9,stroke:#64748B,color:#0F172A
    class A src
    class B sheet
    class C,D,E out
```

### Step 1: the sheet (minutes 0 to 4)

Pick a card. Case A is the default, because its card is written for exactly these three outputs. Run the `source-of-truth-sheet` prompt from [Module 4](../day2/m4-notes-and-audiences.qmd#three-audiences) on the card's bullets.

Then check the sheet against the card, line by line, for the three failures: **invented**, **omitted**, **altered**. Fix it yourself, by hand.

The sheet is now the only source for everything that follows, so an error left here is copied into all three outputs. This is the verification workflow one level up: Draft with AI → Cross-check the source → Confirm or correct → Use. Here the card is the source.

### Steps 2 to 4: make one, check one (5 minutes each) {#make-one-check-one}

Start a new chat for each output and paste the sheet into each one. That way an error in one output cannot leak into the next, and each output draws on the sheet rather than on the others.

| Output | For | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| Chart note | The record, in clinical register | `chart-note-from-sheet`, [Module 4](../day2/m4-notes-and-audiences.qmd#three-audiences) |
| Patient handout | The patient, in plain language | `patient-instructions-from-sheet`, [Module 4](../day2/m4-notes-and-audiences.qmd#three-audiences) |
| Teaching version | Junior colleagues, three slides | `full-talk-slides`, [Module 5](../day2/m5-talks-and-teaching.qmd#full-talk) |

Paste each prompt as taught. Change only its placeholders, and any setting words that do not fit your case (a clinic visit, not an operation). For the slides, paste the sheet under FACTS and type these three titles under OUTLINE: "The case", "What was found", "The plan and the next checks". Three titles give you three slides.

After each output, stop and check three facts against the sheet before you make the next one. Copy this table into your notes. For Case A the three facts are below. For another card, pick a medicine and its dose, a test to repeat and when, and the follow-up interval.

| The fact, from the sheet | Chart note | Handout | Slides |
|---|---|---|---|
| Losartan 50 mg once daily, with amlodipine 5 mg | | | |
| Creatinine and potassium again in 2 weeks | | | |
| Review in 4 weeks | | | |

Tick the box when the output says exactly what the sheet says. If it does not, write one word instead: **altered** (it says something different) or **omitted** (it should be there and is not). A fact left out on purpose, as a handout need not carry every reading, gets a dash.

If two outputs disagree, go to the sheet and the card, not to whichever output reads better. Then ask whether the sheet itself was the source of the error.

Read the handout once more for **invented**: anything it says that the sheet does not. Friendly advice, warnings and reassurance are the usual suspects. Case A names no warning signs to return for. If your handout contains a list of them, it did not come from the card: delete it, or replace it with one you write. A [MISSING: ...] line where the sheet is silent is the prompt doing its job.

### What good looks like

- You fixed the sheet before you made any output.
- Each output was checked before the next one was made.
- Every dose, interval and reading is identical wherever it appears, and copied from the sheet, not re-worked.
- Every box has a tick, a word or a dash. A table with no mismatch is a good result if you checked. A table nobody filled in is not.
- The handout says nothing the sheet does not, is in plain language, and the slides carry no identifiers.

Then type in the chat what your table found: all matched, one differed, or extra content.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
One sheet, three outputs, three facts. An output that disagrees with the sheet is wrong, however fluent it sounds.
:::

## 2. Same source, two tools [10 min]{.time} {#part-2}

**The one change: the tool.** Same source text, same prompt, a general assistant and your second option. The one thing to look for: did it add anything that the source does not say? On Day One you compared two ways of answering ([Lab One, part 3](../day1/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd#part-3)). Now see whether what you found holds on a Day Two task. Glance at your Day One notes first.

### The task

The default is a study summary from the practice source. If you would rather, use a referral letter for [Case C](../reference/case-cards.qmd#case-c) with the referral prompt from [Day One](../day1/m2-prompting.qmd#three-more-jobs). Either way, paste the same prompt, unchanged, into both. If your second option cannot take pasted text (a plain literature search cannot), ask both instead for the evidence behind one number in the practice source, such as the 135/85 threshold, and look at what each lets you check.

<!-- prompt: teaching-summary-from-source | Study summary from a source | Turn a source text into a short, numbers-exact study summary for trainees -->
```text
ROLE: You are a medical educator writing a one-page study summary for [audience, e.g. family medicine residents].
CONTEXT: The summary is for revision. Use ONLY the SOURCE below. If something a learner would need is missing from the SOURCE, write [MISSING: what] instead of adding it.
SOURCE:
[paste the source text]
FORMAT: Exactly [5] bullet points, one per key rule, each starting with its number or threshold in bold. Then one line beginning "Easy to confuse:" naming two rules in the SOURCE with similar numbers. Maximum [120] words.
CONSTRAINTS: Copy every number exactly as written in the SOURCE. Do not add findings, doses, or thresholds that are not in the SOURCE. Cite nothing outside the SOURCE. No hedging phrases.
```

### Look for one thing

- **Minute 0 to 4.** Choose the task, copy the source, and run the prompt in both. If a tool will not take the pasted text, or answers from its own sources instead of yours, write that down. It is a result, not a failure.
- **Minutes 4 to 8.** Read each summary against the source, and fill in the two rows.
- **Minutes 8 to 10.** Finish the two lines under the table.

| | General assistant | Second option |
|---|---|---|
| Added something the source does not say? (yes or no, and what) | | |
| Every number copied exactly? (yes or no) | | |

If a tool cited something, open it before you believe it.

Same pattern as Day One? ______________________

For this job I would use ______________ because ______________________

### What good looks like

- You compared on things you can see: what each added, and whether the numbers match. Not on which answer sounded better.
- If a tool cited something, you opened it before you believed it.
- Your "because" names something you observed, not a feeling about the tool.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
Same task, two ways of answering: look at what each added. Which one sounded better is not a result.
:::

## 3. Share-out [5 min]{.time} {#part-3}

The last five minutes are for doing together what you have been doing alone: applying the check to something a colleague made, in front of the group. It is the same move you will need at work, when someone hands you an AI-drafted note and asks whether it looks fine.

### How it runs

- **Minute 0 to 1.** On your own, choose the one output you would least want to be wrong. The handout is a good candidate, because a patient will act on it. Type "I can share" in the chat if you are willing to show it.
- **Minutes 1 to 4.** The instructor asks two or three of you to share your screen. Each shows the output beside the sheet, reads out two lines, and names one fact checked and where. Everyone else answers the three questions in the chat, yes or no, and the person presenting answers them too:

  1. Could I defend this to a colleague?
  2. Does it point to something I can verify?
  3. Would I catch it if it were wrong?

- **Minute 4 to 5.** Write one thing you will change next time, in the sheet or in the prompt.

If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept. A "no" is a good answer here. What matters is what the presenter does next.

### What good looks like

- The presenter names a specific fact and where they checked it, not "it looked fine".
- A "no" to any question comes with a next step: check the source, or delete the line.
- The group questions the output, not the person presenting it.

### Worksheet

Copy this list into your notes. It is the whole lab on one screen.

- [ ] Card used: ______________
- [ ] Sheet checked line by line against the card. Invented, omitted, altered found: ______________
- [ ] Chart note made, then its three facts checked
- [ ] Handout made, then its three facts checked, and read once for anything invented
- [ ] Slides made, then their three facts checked
- [ ] Same source in two tools: what each added: ______________
- [ ] Share-out: one output presented, three-question check applied
- [ ] One thing I will change next time: ______________

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep this
Fluent is not verified. Say what you checked, against what, and what you would still check.
:::
